tEn: A Newborn, a Neural Net, and Letting Go
tZh: 新生儿、神经网络与放下
sEn: A father discusses his newborn son's name, the parallels between baby brains and AI, and his decision to shed material possessions.
sZh: 一位父亲谈论他新生儿的名字、婴儿大脑与人工智能的相似之处，以及他决定舍弃物质财富。

consensus.en: Possessions weigh you down and are an attack vector; selling them simplifies life and reduces vulnerability.
consensus.zh: 物质财富会拖累你，并成为攻击的靶子；卖掉它们能简化生活并减少脆弱性。

consensus.en: Neuralink aims to solve brain injuries first, then enhance human-AI symbiosis by increasing data transfer rates.
consensus.zh: Neuralink 首先旨在解决脑损伤，然后通过提高数据传输速率来增强人与 AI 的共生关系。

consensus.en: AI will surpass human intelligence; symbiosis is necessary to avoid being left behind.
consensus.zh: AI 将超越人类智能；共生是避免被抛在后面的必要条件。

consensus.en: COVID-19 mortality is much lower than initially feared, especially for younger healthy people.
consensus.zh: COVID-19 的死亡率远低于最初的担忧，尤其是对年轻健康人群。

consensus.en: Government lockdowns are a violation of civil liberties; individuals should have the freedom to choose.
consensus.zh: 政府封锁是对公民自由的侵犯；个人应有选择的自由。

consensus.en: Clear data reporting is essential; separate confirmed COVID cases from symptoms and attribute deaths properly.
consensus.zh: 清晰的数据报告至关重要；区分确诊 COVID 病例与症状，并正确归因死亡原因。

contrarian.en: We are already cyborgs; phones and computers are extensions of ourselves, but data rates are slow.
contrarian.zh: 我们已经是半机械人；手机和电脑是我们自身的延伸，但数据传输速率很慢。

contrarian.en: Language is a lossy compression; direct brain communication could be more precise and faster.
contrarian.zh: 语言是一种有损压缩；直接的大脑通信可能更精确、更快速。

contrarian.en: Selling possessions and not owning houses is better than building a dream house; Mars is more important.
contrarian.zh: 卖掉财产、不拥有房子比建造梦想之家更好；火星更重要。

contrarian.en: The economy is not a magic horn of plenty; if you don't make stuff, there is no stuff.
contrarian.zh: 经济不是丰饶之角；如果你不制造东西，就没有东西。

contrarian.en: COVID death counts are inflated due to financial incentives and loose criteria; data should be parsed.
contrarian.zh: 由于经济激励和宽松标准，COVID 死亡人数被夸大；数据应被细分。

contrarian.en: Eating tasty food and living a shorter life is a valid choice; not everything is about longevity.
contrarian.zh: 吃美味的食物而活得更短是有效的选择；并非一切都关乎长寿。

turns.en: You will never forget what is going on in the world when you think about when your child is born. You will know for the rest of this child's life, you were born during a weird time.
turns.zh: 你永远不会忘记孩子出生时世界上正在发生的事。你会知道，在这个孩子的一生中，他出生在一个奇怪的时代。

turns.en: That's for sure. The probably the weirdest that I can remember.
turns.zh: 那是肯定的。可能是我记忆中最奇怪的了。

turns.en: And he was born on May the 4th. And that's hilarious, too.
turns.zh: 而且他出生在 5 月 4 日。这也太巧了。

turns.en: Yeah. May the 4th be with him.
turns.zh: 是啊。愿 5 月 4 日与他同在。

turns.en: It has to be. I hope so. I sure hope so. Perfect. I mean, that was the perfect day for you.
turns.zh: 必须的。我希望如此。我确实希望如此。完美。我是说，对你来说那是完美的一天。

turns.en: And how do you say the name?
turns.zh: 那名字怎么念？

turns.en: Well, uh...
turns.zh: 嗯，呃……

turns.en: Is it a placeholder?
turns.zh: 是个占位符吗？

turns.en: First of all, my partner is the one that actually mostly came up with the name.
turns.zh: 首先，名字主要是我伴侣想出来的。

turns.en: Congratulations to her.
turns.zh: 恭喜她。

turns.en: Yeah, she's great at names. So, it's just X, the letter X. And then the AE is pronounced 'ash'.
turns.zh: 是啊，她很会起名字。所以就是 X，字母 X。然后 AE 发音是“ash”。

turns.en: And then A-12 is my contribution.
turns.zh: 然后 A-12 是我贡献的。

turns.en: Oh, why A-12?
turns.zh: 哦，为什么是 A-12？

turns.en: Archangel 12, the precursor to the SR-71. Coolest plane ever.
turns.zh: 大天使 12，SR-71 的前身。史上最酷的飞机。

turns.en: It's true. I agree with you. I don't know. I'm not familiar with it. I know what the SR-71 is.
turns.zh: 确实。我同意你。我不知道。我不熟悉它。我知道 SR-71 是什么。

turns.en: So, the SR-71 came from a CIA program called Archangel. Archangel project. And then Archangel 12.
turns.zh: 所以，SR-71 来自一个叫“大天使”的中情局项目。大天使计划。然后是大天使 12。

turns.en: What a dope-looking plane.
turns.zh: 那飞机真酷。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.en: Oh, okay. I get it. Well, as a person who's very much into aerial travel as you are, that's perfect.
turns.zh: 哦，好吧。我懂了。嗯，作为一个像你一样非常喜欢空中旅行的人，那太完美了。

turns.en: It's pretty great.
turns.zh: 挺棒的。

turns.en: So, does it feel strange to have a child while this craziness is going on? You've had children before. Is this any weirder?
turns.zh: 那么，在这种疯狂进行的时候有个孩子，感觉奇怪吗？你以前有过孩子。这次更奇怪吗？

turns.en: It's actually better being older and having a kid. I appreciate it more.
turns.zh: 实际上，年纪大一点有孩子更好。我更珍惜。

turns.en: Mm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: Yeah. Babies are awesome.
turns.zh: 是啊。婴儿太棒了。

turns.en: They are pretty awesome.
turns.zh: 他们确实很棒。

turns.en: They are awesome. Yeah.
turns.zh: 他们很棒。是啊。

turns.en: When I didn't have any of my own, I would see other people's kids and I didn't not like them, but I wasn't drawn to them. But now when I see little people's kids, I'm like, 'Aw.' I think of them as like these little love packages.
turns.zh: 当我自己没有孩子的时候，我看到别人的孩子，我不是不喜欢他们，但也不会被吸引。但现在我看到别人的小孩，我就会“哎呀”。我把他们当成小爱包。

turns.en: Yeah, little love bugs.
turns.zh: 是啊，小爱虫。

turns.en: Yeah, it's just you think of them differently when you see them come out and then grow and then eventually start talking to you. Like your whole idea what a baby is is very different.
turns.zh: 是啊，当你看到他们出生、长大、最终开始和你说话，你对他们的看法就不同了。你对婴儿的整个概念都不一样了。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.en: So now as you get older and get to appreciate it as a mature, fully formed adult, it must be really pretty wonderful.
turns.zh: 所以现在你年纪大了，作为一个成熟、完整的成年人去欣赏它，一定非常美好。

turns.en: Yeah, it's great. But babies are awesome. Yeah, that's great. I've spent a lot of time on AI and neural nets, so you can sort of see the brain develop, which is what an AI neural net is trying to simulate what a brain does, basically. And you can sort of see it learning very quickly. It's just wow.
turns.zh: 是啊，很棒。但婴儿太棒了。是的，那很好。我在 AI 和神经网络上花了很多时间，所以你能看到大脑的发育，而 AI 神经网络基本上就是在模拟大脑的工作。你能看到它学得很快。简直了。

turns.en: So you're talking about the neural net, you're not talking about an actual baby.
turns.zh: 所以你说的是神经网络，不是真正的婴儿。

turns.en: I'm talking about an actual baby.
turns.zh: 我说的是真正的婴儿。

turns.en: But both of them.
turns.zh: 但两者都是。

turns.en: Yes, but the word neural net comes from the brain. It's like a net of neurons. So, you know, it's like the humans are the original gangster neural net.
turns.zh: 是的，但“神经网络”这个词来自大脑。就像神经元网络。所以，你知道，人类就是最初的“黑帮”神经网络。

turns.en: That's a great way to put it.
turns.zh: 这个说法真好。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.en: So when you're programming artificial intelligence or you're working with artificial intelligence, are they specifically trying to mimic the developmental process of a human brain?
turns.zh: 那么当你编程人工智能或与人工智能合作时，它们是在专门模仿人脑的发育过程吗？

turns.en: In a lot of ways. There's some ways that are different. An analogy that's often used is like, we don't make a submarine to look like a fish, but we take the principles of hydrodynamics and apply them to a submarine.
turns.zh: 在很多方面。有些方面是不同的。一个常用的类比是，我们不会把潜艇做成鱼的样子，但我们把流体动力学的原理应用到潜艇上。

turns.en: I've always wondered as a layperson, do you try to achieve the same results as a human brain, but through different methods, or do you try to copy the way a human brain achieves results?
turns.zh: 作为外行，我一直想知道，你们是试图通过不同的方法达到与人脑相同的结果，还是试图复制人脑实现结果的方式？

turns.en: The essential elements of an AI neural net are really very similar to human brain neural net. Having the multiple layers of neurons and back propagation. These all these things are what your brain does. You have a layer of neurons that goes through a series of intermediate steps to ultimately cognition. And then it'll reverse those steps and go back and forth and go all over the place. It's interesting, very interesting.
turns.zh: AI 神经网络的基本要素与人脑神经网络非常相似。有多层神经元和反向传播。这些都是你大脑所做的。你有一层神经元，经过一系列中间步骤最终形成认知。然后它会反转这些步骤，来回反复，到处进行。这很有趣，非常有趣。

turns.en: Yeah, I would imagine like the thought of programming something that is eventually going to be smarter than us. That one day it's going to be like, why did you do it that way? Like when artificial intelligence becomes sentient, they're like, oh, you tried to mimic yourself. Like this so much better process. Cut out all this nonsense.
turns.zh: 是啊，我想象过编程一个最终会比我们更聪明的东西。有一天它会说，你为什么那样做？就像当人工智能有了知觉，它们会说，哦，你试图模仿自己。像这样好得多的过程。去掉所有这些废话。

turns.en: But like I said, there are elements that are the same, but just like an aircraft does not fly like a bird. It doesn't flap its wings. But the way the wings work and generate lift is the same as bird.
turns.zh: 但就像我说的，有些元素是相同的，但就像飞机不像鸟一样飞。它不扇动翅膀。但翅膀产生升力的方式与鸟相同。

turns.en: Now, you're in the middle of this strange time where you're selling your houses. You say you don't want any material possessions and I've been seeing all that and I've been really excited to talk to you about this. Because it's an interesting thing to come from a guy like yourself. Like why are you doing that?
turns.zh: 现在，你正处于这个奇怪的时期，你在卖房子。你说你不想要任何物质财产，我一直看到这些，我真的很兴奋想和你谈谈这个。因为像你这样的人这样做很有趣。你为什么这么做？

turns.en: I'm slightly sad about it, actually.
turns.zh: 实际上，我对此有点难过。

turns.en: Well, then if you're sad about it, why are you doing it?
turns.zh: 嗯，如果你难过，为什么还要做？

turns.en: I think possessions kind of weigh you down. They're kind of an attack vector. You know, they'll say, 'Hey billionaire, you got all this stuff.' Like, well, now I don't have stuff. Now what are you going to do?
turns.zh: 我认为财产会拖累你。它们是一种攻击向量。你知道，他们会说，“嘿，亿万富翁，你有这么多东西。”就像，好吧，现在我没有东西了。现在你怎么办？

turns.en: Attack vector meaning like people target it.
turns.zh: 攻击向量是指人们针对它。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Mhm, interesting. Yeah. But you're obviously going to rent a place?
turns.zh: 嗯，有趣。是的。但你显然会租个地方？

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Okay. And get rid of everything except clothes?
turns.zh: 好的。然后除了衣服，什么都不要？

turns.en: No, I sold like almost everything. So it's like keep a couple Teslas. Yeah, sure. I have to keep a Tesla. Kind of have to. Test product and stuff. There are things that have sentimental value, for sure. Keeping those, yeah.
turns.zh: 不，我几乎卖掉了所有东西。所以就像留几辆特斯拉。是的，当然。我必须留一辆特斯拉。算是必须的。测试产品之类的。当然有些东西有情感价值。那些会留着，是的。

turns.en: So do you feel like...
turns.zh: 那你觉得……

turns.en: I mean what's the worst that could happen? I mean, we'll be fine.
turns.zh: 我是说，最坏能发生什么？我们不会有事的。

turns.en: Yeah, yeah. You could always buy more stuff if you don't like it.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊。如果你不喜欢，你总能买更多东西。

turns.en: Suppose so.
turns.zh: 我想也是。

turns.en: Yeah, I mean from the money that you sell all your stuff, you could buy new stuff.
turns.zh: 是啊，我是说用你卖掉所有东西的钱，你可以买新东西。

turns.en: But do you feel like people define you by the fact that you're wealthy? And that they define you in a pejorative way?
turns.zh: 但你觉得人们会因为你有钱而定义你吗？而且是以一种贬义的方式定义你？

turns.en: For sure. I mean, not everyone, but you know, there's, for sure in recent years, billionaire has become a pejorative—like it's a bad thing. Which I think doesn't make a lot of sense in most cases. If you've basically organized a company—like, how does this wealth arise? It's if you organize people in a better way to produce products and services that are better than what existed before, and you have some ownership in that company, then that essentially gives you the right to allocate more capital. So there's a conflation of consumption and capital allocation. So, I mean, say Warren Buffett, for example. And to be totally frank, I'm not his biggest fan, but he does like capital allocation. And he reads a lot of annual reports of companies and accounting, and it's pretty boring, really. And he's trying to figure out: does Coke or Pepsi deserve more capital? I mean, it's kind of a boring job, if you ask me. But it's still a thing that's important to figure out—whether a company is deserving of more or less capital, should that company grow or expand, is it making products and services that are better than others or worse? And if a company is making compelling products and services, it should get more capital, and if it's not, it should get less or go out of business.
turns.zh: 当然。我是说，不是所有人，但你知道，近年来“亿万富翁”确实变成了一个贬义词——好像那是件坏事。我觉得在大多数情况下这没什么道理。如果你基本上组织了一家公司——这财富是怎么来的？如果你以更好的方式组织人们，生产出比以前更好的产品和服务，而你在那家公司拥有一些所有权，那本质上就赋予了你分配更多资本的权利。所以这里混淆了消费和资本分配。比如沃伦·巴菲特。坦白说，我不是他的最大粉丝，但他确实喜欢资本分配。他读很多公司的年报和会计报告，那真的很无聊。他试图弄清楚：可口可乐还是百事可乐更值得获得更多资本？我是说，在我看来这有点无聊。但弄清楚一家公司是否值得更多或更少的资本，那家公司是否应该增长或扩张，它是否在制造比别人更好或更差的产品和服务，这仍然是重要的事。如果一家公司制造出有吸引力的产品和服务，它就应该得到更多资本；如果不是，就应该得到更少，或者倒闭。

turns.en: Well, there's a big difference too between someone who's making an incredible amount of money designing and engineering fantastic products versus someone who's making an incredible amount of money by investing in companies or moving money around in the stock market or doing things along those lines. It's a different thing, and to put them all in the same category seems very simple. And as you pointed out, it's an attack vector.
turns.zh: 嗯，设计并工程化出绝佳产品而赚大钱的人，和通过投资公司或在股市里倒腾资金而赚大钱的人，这两者之间也有很大区别。这是不同的东西，把它们都归为一类似乎太简单了。而且正如你指出的，这是一个攻击点。

turns.en: Yeah, for sure.
turns.zh: 是的，当然。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: I mean, I think it's really—I do think there, in the United States especially, there's an overallocation of talent in finance and law. Basically, too many smart people go into finance and law. So, you know, this is both a compliment and a criticism. We should have, I think, fewer people doing law and fewer people doing finance, and more people making stuff.
turns.zh: 我是说，我觉得真的——我确实认为，尤其是在美国，金融和法律领域的人才配置过度了。基本上，太多聪明人进入了金融和法律。所以，你知道，这既是赞美也是批评。我认为我们应该让更少的人做法律，更少的人做金融，而让更多的人去制造东西。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: Well, that would certainly be better for all involved if they made better stuff.
turns.zh: 嗯，如果他们做出更好的东西，那对所有相关方来说肯定会更好。

turns.en: Yeah, yeah, absolutely. And manufacturing used to be highly valued in the United States, and these days it's not—it's often looked down upon, which I think is wrong.
turns.zh: 是的，是的，绝对。而且制造业在美国曾经备受重视，如今却不是了——常常被看不起，我觉得这是不对的。

turns.en: Yeah. Well, I think that people are kind of learning that, particularly because of this whole pandemic and this relationship that we have with China, that there's a lot of value in making things, and making things here.
turns.zh: 是的。嗯，我觉得人们正在慢慢认识到这一点，尤其是因为这场疫情和我们与中国的关系，制造东西、在这里制造东西，有很多价值。

turns.en: Yes, somebody's got to do the real work.
turns.zh: 是的，总得有人做真正的工作。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: You know, and making a car—it's an honest day's living, that's for sure. Or making anything really, or providing valuable service, like providing good entertainment, good information. These are all valuable things to do. So yeah, there should be more of it.
turns.zh: 你知道，造一辆车——那是诚实的谋生方式，这是肯定的。或者制造任何东西，或者提供有价值的服务，比如提供好的娱乐、好的信息。这些都是有价值的事情。所以是的，应该有更多这样的工作。

turns.en: Did you have a moment where this idea of getting rid of your material possessions built up over time, or did you have a moment of realization?
turns.zh: 你有没有一个时刻，这个摆脱物质财产的想法是逐渐积累起来的，还是你有一个顿悟的时刻？

turns.en: Yeah, I've been thinking about it for a while. Part of it is like I have a bunch of houses, but I don't spend a lot of time in most of them, and that doesn't seem like a good use of assets. Somebody could probably be enjoying those houses and get better use of them than me, so.
turns.zh: 是的，我一直在考虑这件事。部分原因是，我有很多房子，但大部分我都不怎么住，这似乎不是对资产的良好利用。也许有人能享受那些房子，比我更好地利用它们，所以。

turns.en: Don't you have Gene Wilder's house?
turns.zh: 你不是有吉恩·怀尔德（Gene Wilder）的房子吗？

turns.en: I do.
turns.zh: 我有。

turns.en: That's amazing.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.en: It's awesome.
turns.zh: 那房子很棒。

turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.en: Yeah, it's exactly what you'd expect.
turns.zh: 是的，它正是你所期望的那样。

turns.en: Did you request that the buyer not tear it up?
turns.zh: 你有没有要求买家不要拆掉它？

turns.en: Yeah, that's a requirement.
turns.zh: 是的，那是一个要求。

turns.en: Oh, a requirement. That's a good requirement.
turns.zh: 哦，一个要求。那是个好要求。

turns.en: In that case, in that house.
turns.zh: 在那个情况下，在那栋房子里。

turns.en: Yeah, it'll probably sell for less, but still I don't care.
turns.zh: 是的，它可能会卖得更便宜，但我还是不在乎。

turns.en: He's a legend.
turns.zh: 他是个传奇。

turns.en: Yeah, he's a legend. His soul—you'd want his essence in the building.
turns.zh: 是的，他是个传奇。他的灵魂——你会希望他的精髓留在那栋建筑里。

turns.en: It's there. It's a real quirky house, yeah.
turns.zh: 它就在那里。那真是一栋古怪的房子，是的。

turns.en: What makes you say that? Like what do you get out of it?
turns.zh: 你为什么这么说？你从中得到了什么？

turns.en: All the cabinets are handmade and they're like odd shapes, and there's like doors to nowhere and strange corridors and tunnels, and odd paintings on the wall. Yeah.
turns.zh: 所有的橱柜都是手工制作的，形状古怪，还有通往无处可去的门、奇怪的走廊和隧道，墙上挂着古怪的画。是的。

turns.en: Really?
turns.zh: 真的吗？

turns.zh: 是的，我看到了那个。它火了。

turns.en: Is that monkey conscious? It seems like it is. It seems like it had a plan. It was riding a motorcycle and it jumped off and tried to steal a baby. Seems pretty conscious.
turns.zh: 那只猴子有意识吗？看起来是的。看起来它有一个计划。它骑着摩托车，跳下来试图偷一个婴儿。看起来相当有意识。

turns.en: The one that just dragged a baby down the street pretty far.
turns.zh: 那个把婴儿拖了很远的那个。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: Seems pretty conscious. Right?
turns.zh: 看起来相当有意识。对吧？

turns.en: There's definitely some degree of consciousness there.
turns.zh: 那里肯定有一定程度的意识。

turns.en: Yeah, it's not like it's a worm.
turns.zh: 是的，它不像一条虫子。

turns.en: It's not.
turns.zh: 它不是。

turns.en: It's on another level. And it's going to keep going, and that's the real concern when people think about potential future versions of human beings, especially when you consider symbiotic relationship to artificial intelligence that will be unrecognizable. That one day we'll be so far removed from what this is, we'll look back on this the way we look back now on simple organisms that we evolved from. And it won't be that far in the future that we do have this view back.
turns.zh: 它是在另一个层次上。而且它会继续发展，当人们想到人类可能的未来版本时，这是真正的担忧，尤其是当你考虑到与人工智能的共生关系时，那将是无法辨认的。有一天我们会离现在这个状态如此遥远，我们会回顾现在，就像我们现在回顾我们进化而来的简单生物一样。而且我们拥有这种回顾视角不会太遥远。

turns.en: Well, I hope consciousness propagates into the future and gets more sophisticated and complex, and that it understands the questions to ask about the universe.
turns.zh: 嗯，我希望意识能传播到未来，变得更复杂、更精细，并且它能理解关于宇宙要问的问题。

turns.en: Do you think that's the case? As a human being, you're clearly trying to make conscious decisions to be a better version of you, right? This is the idea of getting rid of your possessions and realizing that you're trying to improve. I don't like this, I will try to improve this. I will try to do a better version of the way I interface with reality. This is always the way things are if you're moving in a direction where you're trying to improve things, you're always going to move into this new place where you look back at the old place and go, 'Ah, I was doing it wrong back then.' So, this is an accelerated version of that. A super accelerated version of that.
turns.zh: 你觉得是这样吗？作为一个人，你显然在努力做出有意识的决定，成为更好的自己，对吧？这就是摆脱你的财产并意识到你在努力改进的想法。我不喜欢这个，我会努力改进这个。我会努力以更好的方式与现实互动。如果你朝着改进的方向前进，事情总是这样，你总是会进入一个新的地方，回顾旧的地方，然后说，‘啊，我当时做错了。’所以，这是一个加速版本。一个超级加速版本。

turns.en: I mean, you don't always improve, but you can aspire to improve. You can aspire to be less wrong.
turns.zh: 我是说，你并不总是改进，但你可以渴望改进。你可以渴望少犯错。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: This is like, I think, a good tool. The tools of physics are very powerful. Just assume you're wrong, and your goal is to be less wrong. I don't think you're going to succeed every day in being less wrong, but if you're going to succeed in being less wrong most of the time, you're doing great.
turns.zh: 这就像，我认为，一个好的工具。物理学的工具非常强大。只要假设你是错的，你的目标是少犯错。我不认为你每天都会成功地少犯错，但如果你大多数时候都能成功地少犯错，你就做得很好。

turns.en: That's a great way of putting it, aspire to be less wrong.
turns.zh: 这是一个很好的说法，渴望少犯错。

turns.en: Mhm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: But then when people look back in nostalgia about simpler times, there's that too. It's very romantic and exciting to look back on campfires.
turns.zh: 但当人们怀旧地回顾更简单的时代时，也有那一点。回顾篝火是非常浪漫和令人兴奋的。

turns.en: But you can still have a campfire.
turns.zh: 但你仍然可以生篝火。

turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: But will you appreciate it when you're a super nerd? When you connect it to the grid and you have some skull cap in place of the top of your head and it's interfacing with the international language that the rest of the universe now enjoys, communicating with people?
turns.zh: 但当你成为一个超级极客时，你会欣赏它吗？当你把它连接到电网，你有一个 skull cap 代替你的头顶，它与宇宙其他部分现在享受的国际语言接口，与人交流？

turns.en: Yeah, sure. I think so.
turns.zh: 是的，当然。我想是的。

turns.en: Uh yeah, I like campfires.
turns.zh: 嗯，我喜欢篝火。

turns.en: I'm just worried—I mean, everyone's always scared of change, but I'm scared of this monumental change where we won't talk anymore.
turns.zh: 我只是担心——我是说，大家都害怕变化，但我害怕的是这种巨变，我们不再交谈了。

turns.en: I mean that thing you just—
turns.zh: 我是说你刚才说的那个——

turns.en: Yes, but there's something about the beauty of the crudeness of language where when it's done eloquently, it's satisfying, and it hits us in some sort of a visceral way, like 'Ah, that person nailed it.' I love that they nailed it like that. It's so hard to capture a real thought and convey it in an articulate way that makes someone excited. Like you read a quote, a great quote by a wise person. It makes you excited that their mind figured something out, put the words together in the right way that makes your brain pop. Like, 'Oh yes.'
turns.zh: 是的，但语言粗粝之美在于，当它被雄辩地表达出来时，会让人满足，并以某种本能的方式击中我们，比如“啊，那人说得太到位了。”我喜欢那种精准。要捕捉一个真实的想法，并以一种让人兴奋的清晰方式传达出来，太难了。比如你读到一句名言，一位智者说的妙语。你会兴奋，因为他们的头脑想通了某件事，把词语以正确的方式组合起来，让你的大脑为之一振。就像“哦，没错。”

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: It's clever compression of a concept.
turns.zh: 这是对概念的巧妙压缩。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: And a feeling.
turns.zh: 还有情感。

turns.en: But the fact that a human did it, too.
turns.zh: 但这也是人类做到的。

turns.en: Absolutely.
turns.zh: 绝对。

turns.en: Do you think that it'll be like electronic music? Like people won't appreciate it like they appreciate a slide guitar?
turns.zh: 你觉得这会像电子音乐吗？人们不会像欣赏滑棒吉他那样欣赏它？

turns.en: I like electronic music.
turns.zh: 我喜欢电子音乐。

turns.en: I do, too.
turns.zh: 我也喜欢。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: Well, you make it. I know you like it.
turns.zh: 好吧，你制作电子音乐。我知道你喜欢。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: Yeah. I mean, I hope the future is more fun and interesting, and we're just trying to make it that way.
turns.zh: 嗯。我是说，我希望未来更有趣、更精彩，我们正努力让它变成那样。

turns.en: I hope it's more fun and interesting, too.
turns.zh: 我也希望它更有趣、更精彩。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: I just hope we don't lose anything along the way.
turns.zh: 我只是希望我们不会在过程中失去什么。

turns.en: I mean, we might lose a little, but hopefully we'll gain more than we lose.
turns.zh: 我是说，我们可能会失去一点，但希望我们得到的比失去的多。

turns.en: Yeah, that's the thing, right? Gaining more than we lose. Like something that makes us interesting is that we're so flawed.
turns.zh: 嗯，这就是关键，对吧？得到比失去多。比如让我们有趣的一点就是我们如此不完美。

turns.en: That's for sure.
turns.zh: 那当然。

turns.en: Mhm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: I mean, you look at civilization through the ages, most of them rose and fell.
turns.zh: 我是说，纵观历代文明，大多数都兴衰更替。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: And I do think that the globalization that we have at this sort of like the meme sphere is that there's not enough isolation between countries or regions. It's like if there's a mind virus, that mind virus can infect too much of the world. You know, I actually sort of sympathize with the anti-globalization people, because it's like, man, we don't want everyone everywhere to be the same, for sure. And then we need some kind of mind viral immunity.
turns.zh: 而且我确实认为，我们在这种类似模因领域拥有的全球化，意味着国家或地区之间没有足够的隔离。就像如果有一种思想病毒，那种思想病毒可以感染世界上太多地方。你知道，我其实有点同情反全球化的人，因为就像，天哪，我们肯定不希望所有地方的人都一样。然后我们需要某种思想病毒免疫力。

turns.en: Mhm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: So that's a bit concerning.
turns.zh: 所以这有点令人担忧。

turns.en: Mind viral immunity meaning that once something like Neuralink gets established, the real concern is something that—I mean you said it's Bluetooth, right? Or some future version of that. That the idea is that something could possibly get into it, mess it up.
turns.zh: 思想病毒免疫力，意思是像 Neuralink 这样的东西一旦建立，真正的担忧是——我是说你说过它是蓝牙，对吧？或者某种未来版本。就是说某种东西可能侵入它，搞乱它。

turns.en: No, I'm talking about like somebody that's some cockeyed concept that happens right now.
turns.zh: 不，我说的是像某种荒谬的概念，现在就在发生。

turns.en: Mhm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: You know.
turns.zh: 你知道。

turns.en: Well, I know this virus is in embedded chips, right? Like people have embedded chips and then acquired viruses.
turns.zh: 好吧，我知道这种病毒在嵌入式芯片里，对吧？比如人们植入了芯片，然后感染了病毒。

turns.en: Well, when I'm talking about a mind virus, I'm talking about a concept that infects people's minds.
turns.zh: 好吧，当我说思想病毒时，我说的是感染人们思想的概念。

turns.en: Oh, okay. Like cult thinking or some sort of fundamentalism.
turns.zh: 哦，好的。比如邪教思维或某种原教旨主义。

turns.en: Yeah, just some wrong-headed idea that goes viral in an idea sense.
turns.zh: 是的，就是一些错误的想法，在观念层面像病毒一样传播。

turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Mhm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: Well, that is a problem, too, right? If someone can manipulate that technology to make something appear logical or rational.
turns.zh: 好吧，那也是问题，对吧？如果有人能操纵那种技术，让某件事看起来合乎逻辑或理性。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: That would be an issue, too, with—this is a very have versus have-not issue. Right? Once this thing—if this really does—I mean, initially, it's going to help people with injuries, but you said ultimately, it could lead to this spectacular cognitive change.
turns.zh: 那也会是个问题，而且——这是一个非常“有与无”的问题。对吧？一旦这东西——如果它真的——我是说，最初它会帮助受伤的人，但你说过最终它可能导致这种惊人的认知改变。

turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: But the people that first get it should have a massive advantage over people that don't have it yet.
turns.zh: 但最先得到它的人应该比还没有它的人有巨大优势。

turns.en: Well, I mean, it's the kind of thing where your productivity would improve dramatically, maybe by a factor of 10 with it. So, you could definitely just, you know, take out a loan and do it and earn the money back real fast.
turns.zh: 好吧，我是说，这种东西会让你的生产力大幅提升，也许提升 10 倍。所以，你完全可以，你知道，贷款去做，然后很快赚回钱。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: Super smart.
turns.zh: 超级聪明。

turns.en: Well, in a capitalist society, you know, you could—it seems like you could really get so far ahead that before everybody else could afford this thing and link up and get connected as well, you'd be so far ahead they could never catch you. Is that a concern?
turns.zh: 好吧，在资本主义社会，你知道，你可能会——看起来你真的能领先那么多，以至于在其他人买得起这东西并连接起来之前，你已经领先到他们永远追不上。这是不是个担忧？

turns.en: Well, I think—I mean, it's not a super huge concern. I mean, there are huge differences in cognitive ability and resources already.
turns.zh: 好吧，我觉得——我是说，这不是一个超级大的担忧。我是说，认知能力和资源方面已经存在巨大差异。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: I mean, you can think of a corporation as like a cybernetic collective that's far smarter than an individual. Like, I couldn't personally build a whole rocket, and the engines, and launch it, and everything. That's impossible. But you know, we have 8,000 people at SpaceX, and piecing it out to different people, and using computers and machines and stuff, we can make lots of rockets launch into orbit, dock with the space station, that kind of thing. So that already exists, where corporations are vastly more capable than an individual. But we should be less concerned about relative capabilities between people, and more about having AI be vastly beyond us and decoupled from human will.
turns.zh: 我是说，你可以把公司想象成一个控制论集体，比个人聪明得多。比如，我个人无法建造整枚火箭、发动机，并发射它，等等。那是不可能的。但你知道，SpaceX 有 8000 人，把任务分给不同的人，利用计算机和机器等，我们可以让很多火箭发射入轨，与空间站对接，诸如此类。所以那已经存在，公司比个人强大得多。但我们应该更少担心人与人之间的相对能力，而更多担心 AI 远远超越我们，并与人类意志脱钩。

turns.en: Decoupled from human will. So, this is the 'if you can't beat them, join them.'
turns.zh: 与人类意志脱钩。所以，这就是“打不过就加入”。

turns.en: Yeah, I mean—
turns.zh: 是的，我是说——

turns.en: Do you feel like it's inevitable? Like AI, sentient AI is essentially inevitable.
turns.zh: 你觉得这是不可避免的吗？比如有感知的 AI 基本上是不可避免的。

turns.en: Super sentient AI, yeah. Like beyond a level that's difficult to understand.
turns.zh: 超级有感知的 AI，是的。就像超越一个难以理解的水平。

turns.en: And—
turns.zh: 而且——

turns.en: To understand, probably.
turns.zh: 难以理解，很可能。

turns.en: And somehow or another, it's almost like it's a requirement for survival to achieve some sort of symbiotic existence with AI.
turns.zh: 而且不知怎么地，这几乎像是为了生存，必须与 AI 实现某种共生关系。

turns.en: It's not a requirement. It's just—if you want to be along for the ride, then you need to do some kind of symbiosis. So, the way your brain works right now, you've got kind of like the animal brain, reptile brain, like the limbic system, basically. And you've got the cortex. Now, the brain purist will argue with this definition, but essentially, you've got the primitive brain and you've got the sort of smart brain, or the brain that's capable of planning and understanding concepts and different difficult things that a monkey can't understand. Now, your cortex is much, much smarter than your limbic system. Nonetheless, they work together well. So, I haven't met anyone who wants to delete the limbic system or the cortex.
turns.zh: 这不是必须的。只是——如果你想搭上这趟车，那么你需要某种共生。所以，你现在大脑的工作方式，你有类似动物脑、爬虫脑，基本上是边缘系统。你还有皮层。现在，脑科学纯粹主义者会争论这个定义，但本质上，你有原始脑，还有那种聪明的脑，或者能够规划、理解概念和猴子无法理解的困难事物的脑。现在，你的皮层比边缘系统聪明得多。尽管如此，它们合作得很好。所以，我还没遇到谁想删除边缘系统或皮层。

turns.en: The people are quite happy having both. So, you can think of this as the computer or AI being like a third layer or tertiary layer. It could be symbiotic with the cortex. It would be much smarter than the cortex. But essentially, you have three layers. And you actually have that right now. Your phone is capable of things and your computer is capable of things that your brain is definitely not. Storing terabytes of information perfectly, doing incredible calculations that we couldn't even come close to doing. You have that with your computer. It's just like I said, the data rate is slow. The connection is weak.
turns.zh: 人们很乐意两者兼得。所以，你可以把这看作是计算机或 AI 作为第三层或第三级。它可以与大脑皮层共生。它会比大脑皮层聪明得多。但本质上，你有三层。而且你现在实际上就有。你的手机能做的事情，你的电脑能做的事情，你的大脑绝对做不到。完美存储 TB 级信息，进行我们根本无法企及的惊人计算。你的电脑就能做到。就像我说的，只是数据传输速率慢，连接很弱。

turns.en: Why is it so disconcerting? Or why does it not give me comfort to think about a symbiotic connection to AI? I always think of this cold, emotionless sort of thing that we will become. Is that a bad way to look at it?
turns.zh: 为什么这让人如此不安？或者为什么想到与 AI 的共生连接并不能让我感到安慰？我总会想到我们会变成那种冰冷、没有感情的东西。这样想是不是不对？

turns.en: I don't think that's correct. That's not how it would be. Like I said, you already are symbiotic with AI or computers.
turns.zh: 我觉得那不对。不会是这样的。就像我说的，你已经与 AI 或计算机共生。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: Phones, computers, laptops.
turns.zh: 手机、电脑、笔记本。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: And there's quite a bit of AI going on, you know, neural nets. Artificial neural nets. Increasingly, neural nets are taking over from regular programming more and more. So, you are connected. If you use Google Voice or Alexa or one of those things, it's using a neural net to decode your speech and try to understand what you're saying. If you're trying to do image recognition or improve the quality of a photograph, it's using neural nets, the best way to do that. So you are already sort of a cybernetic symbiont. It's just a question of your data rate. The communication speed between your phone and your brain is slow.
turns.zh: 而且有很多 AI 在运行，你知道，神经网络。人工神经网络。神经网络正越来越多地取代常规编程。所以，你是连接着的。如果你用 Google Voice 或 Alexa 之类的，它就是用神经网络来解码你的语音，试图理解你在说什么。如果你想做图像识别或提高照片质量，就是用神经网络，这是最好的方式。所以你已经是一种控制论共生体了。只是数据传输速率的问题。你的手机和大脑之间的通信速度很慢。

turns.en: When do you think you're going to do it? How long will you wait?
turns.zh: 你觉得你什么时候会做？你会等多久？

turns.en: Um...
Like once it starts becoming available.
turns.zh: 比如一旦它开始可用。

turns.en: Yeah, if it works, I'll do it, sure.
turns.zh: 对，如果它有效，我会做的，当然。

turns.en: Right away?
turns.zh: 马上？

turns.en: I mean, let's make sure it works.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，先确保它有效。

turns.en: How do we make sure it works? We try it on prisoners? Like what do you do?
turns.zh: 我们怎么确保它有效？在囚犯身上试？你们怎么做？

turns.en: No, no, you...
turns.zh: 不，不，你……

turns.en: Take rapists?
turns.zh: 拿强奸犯？

turns.en: No.
turns.zh: 不。

turns.en: Cut holes in their head?
turns.zh: 在他们头上打洞？

turns.en: Like I said, if somebody's got a serious brain injury...
turns.zh: 就像我说的，如果有人有严重的脑损伤……

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: And there are people with very severe brain injuries. And then you can fix those brain injuries. And then you prove out that it works and you expand the envelope, expand and make more and more brain injuries. It's sold more and more. And then, at some age, we all are going to get Alzheimer's. We're all going to get senile. And then moms forget the names of their kids and that kind of thing. So, this would allow you to remember the names of your kids and have a much more normal life where you're able to function much later in life. So essentially, almost everyone would find a need at some point if you get old enough to use your neural link.
